title: A Home That Isn't a Bunker
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 35 of 40
content:
Bravo was defensible.

It was also underground, windowless, damp, and slowly turning both of us into creatures who argued about ventilation.

“We need to move,” I said.

Danse looked up from the generator manual.

“Why?”

“Mold.”

“Where?”

I pointed to the corner.

“That could be discoloration.”

“It has texture.”

He stood immediately.

Two days later we were looking at an abandoned roadside house near a small settlement.

It had half a roof, no door, one intact wall, and a tree growing through the kitchen.

Danse stared at it.

“No.”

“It has windows.”

“It has weather inside.”

“Temporary.”

“The foundation is cracked.”

“Repairable.”

“There’s a radroach nest in the bathroom.”

“Evictable.”

He looked at me.

“You want this place.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

I looked through the missing wall at the field beyond.

“Because it doesn’t feel borrowed.”

That changed his expression.

Bravo had belonged to the Brotherhood.

So had the Prydwen.

So had every bunk Danse had slept in for years.

He turned back to the ruin.

“The roof will need complete replacement.”

I smiled.

“Is that a yes?”

“It’s an assessment.”

“Danse.”

He sighed.

“Yes.”

We spent three weeks rebuilding.

Danse planned everything.

I ignored approximately thirty percent of the plans.

He complained.

Then admitted some of my changes were better.

This may have been the most significant evidence of character growth in the entire Commonwealth.

We salvaged lumber, patched the foundation, cleared the radroaches, rebuilt the chimney, and installed a water pump outside.

Danse built a weapon bench along one wall of the new workshop.

I built shelves.

He rebuilt my shelves.

I threatened him with a hammer.

He kissed me.

This was effective conflict resolution.

The first night the roof was fully sealed, rain began.

We sat on the floor because we did not own enough furniture.

A lantern burned between us.

Water struck the new roof in a steady rhythm.

Danse looked upward every few seconds.

“It’s holding.”

“I told you it would.”

“The western seam may need another layer.”

“It is not leaking.”

“Yet.”

I handed him a mug.

“Drink.”

He did.

His face changed.

“This coffee is good.”

“Yes.”

“How?”

“I made it.”

He looked betrayed.

I laughed.

The house smelled like fresh-cut wood, damp earth, coffee, and the faint ozone scent of Danse’s charging equipment.

It smelled like work.

Ours.

Danse leaned back against the wall.

“I’ve never had this.”

“A roof?”

“A home that wasn’t assigned.”

The humor left me.

I rested my head on his shoulder.

“You have one now.”

He looked around the half-empty room.

“What makes it a home?”

“You really want me to answer that?”

“Yes.”

I thought about it.

“The fact that we can choose to leave.”

Danse was quiet.

Then nodded.

“That makes sense.”

“And the coffee.”

“The coffee helps.”

“And the radroaches we murdered together.”

“Important shared experience.”

“And you.”

He looked at me.

“And you,” he said.

Rain filled the silence.

Danse kissed my temple.

Outside, the Commonwealth remained dangerous, irradiated, violent, unresolved.

Inside, the roof held.

Moving out of Bravo took longer than rebuilding the house.

Danse had accumulated objects without realizing they were possessions.

A cracked mug from Cambridge.

Two notebooks full of maintenance diagrams.

The detective novel.

The guitar.

The red scarf, though that stayed on him.

Three different weapon-cleaning kits because apparently each had a unique and necessary function.

“You own things,” I told him.

“I require equipment.”

“You own four shirts.”

“Clothing is equipment.”

“You own a book with a terrible detective.”

“Reference material.”

“You own a guitar.”

He looked cornered.

“Morale equipment.”

I laughed.

We packed everything anyway.

The last object was the Brotherhood undersuit.

Danse stood before the open storage trunk for a long time.

I stayed by the door.

“Want privacy?”

“No.”

He lifted the folded fabric.

The insignia looked almost black in the bunker light.

“I wore this the day we met.”

“Under about eight hundred pounds of armor.”

“Closer to a thousand, depending on configuration.”

“Of course you know the number.”

His mouth moved faintly.

Then the humor faded.

“I don’t want to leave it here.”

“Then don’t.”

“I also don’t want it hanging in the new house like a shrine.”

“Then put it in a drawer.”

He looked at me.

“You make things sound simple.”

“No. I make this part simple. You can keep an object without deciding what every memory attached to it means.”

Danse considered that.

He packed the uniform.

When we stepped into the elevator with the final crate, he stopped before pressing the control.

Bravo hummed around us.

The bunker had nearly become his grave.

Then his refuge.

Then, for a while, the only place he believed he was allowed to exist.

“You ready?” I asked.

“No.”

“Good answer.”

He pressed the button.

The doors closed.

We left anyway.

At the house, everything looked unfinished and alive.

Tools on the floor. A patch of plaster still drying. Two chairs that did not match. One window pane made from clear plastic because real glass was too expensive.

Danse carried the first crate into the workshop.

“Where?”

“Wherever you want.”

He frowned at the room.

“Stop doing that.”

“What?”

“Making me choose.”

“No.”

He sighed.

Then set the crate beneath the left workbench.

A choice.

By evening the house had changed.

His books sat on a shelf. The guitar leaned beside a chair. The coffee maker occupied the counter with the confidence of a hostile occupying force.

I hammered two hooks by the door.

Danse inspected them.

“They’re uneven.”

“They’re charming.”

“They’re visibly uneven.”

“Hang your jacket on one and you won’t see it.”

He stared at me.

Then hung the jacket.

I won.

We made dinner on the repaired stove.

The first attempt burned because we got distracted arguing over whether the chimney draw was sufficient.

The second was edible.

Afterward Danse stood at the front window looking toward the settlement lights.

“No perimeter wall,” he said.

“There’s a fence.”

“Decorative.”

“We can improve it.”

“No firing position on the roof.”

“We are not installing a firing position on the roof.”

“We should at least consider—”

“No.”

Danse looked personally wounded.

“This is the Commonwealth.”

“It is also our house.”

“Those concepts are not mutually exclusive.”

I stepped beside him.

“Can we have one place designed first for living and second for surviving?”

His expression changed.

That was harder than arguing about architecture.

After a moment he nodded.

“One reinforced shutter per window.”

“Fine.”

“Emergency weapons cache.”

“One.”

“Two.”

“One and a half.”

“What is half a weapons cache?”

“I don’t know. Compromise.”

He laughed.

We shook on it like idiots.

The first meal in the house was eggs cooked over a camp stove because the kitchen still lacked a working range.

Danse sat on an upside-down crate and surveyed the room like a commander inspecting a battlefield.

“One wall needs reinforcement.”

“Yes.”

“The western window leaks.”

“Yes.”

“The roof patch over the hall is temporary.”

“Yes.”

He looked down at his plate.

“The eggs are good.”

I smiled.

“Thank you.”

Wind moved through the open doorway. Somewhere outside, a settlement dog barked.

Danse ate another bite.

“This is inefficient.”

“The house?”

“Rebuilding it.”

“Compared to Bravo?”

“Yes. Bravo already has reinforced walls, power, defensive position—”

“And mold.”

“And mold.”

“Still want to go back?”

He looked around again.

The half-finished shelves. The repaired window. Our two mugs on the counter. His detective novel on the sill. The guitar leaning against the wall because there was nowhere sensible to put it yet.

“No,” he said.

That was when the place started becoming home.

Before dark, Danse installed three locks on the front door.

“Three?”

“One is damaged.”

“Then replace the damaged one.”

“I will.”

“So why install it?”

“Temporary redundancy.”

I leaned against the frame and watched him work.

“You know home is allowed to be secure without becoming a bunker.”

His hands paused.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He looked out through the open window at the settlement lights beginning to appear below us.

“I’m trying to.”

He removed the damaged lock.

We kept two.

We carried the last crate inside together. Danse set it down, looked around the unfinished room, and said, almost to himself, “We can improve this.”

Not *secure it.* Not *fortify it.* Improve it.

I loved the difference.

That night the bedroom felt too open after Bravo. Moonlight came through the window. Wind moved the curtains. Every outside sound reached us.

Danse lay awake beside me.

“Too exposed?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“Want to go back?”

He thought.

“No.”

I took his hand beneath the blanket.

A branch tapped the siding.

Danse flinched, then sighed at himself.

“You can check it.”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

The branch tapped again.

He stared at the ceiling.

“This may take time.”

“We have some.”

His fingers tightened around mine.

By midnight he was asleep.

I woke before dawn and found him still there, face softened by rest, red scarf draped over the back of a chair, rifle within reach but not in his hands.

Through the window, the first light touched the roof we had built.

It held.

So did we.
